entries.82bd3581b8a85e2b3a51da0faebfc26cc8ab2ac2: <div sID="gen6576" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1Kgs.4" sID="1Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen6576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6577" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6578" type="x-p"/> An instance of the wisdom God granted to Solomon we had in the close of the foregoing chapter. In this we have an account of his wealth and prosperity, the other branch of the promise there made him. We have here, I. The magnificence of his court, his ministers of state (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.1-1Kgs.4.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), and the purveyors of his household (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.7-1Kgs.4.19">ver. 7-19</reference>), and their office, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.27-1Kgs.4.28">ver. 27, 28</reference>. II. The provisions for his table, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.22-1Kgs.4.23">ver. 22, 23</reference>. III. The extent of his dominion, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21-1Kgs.4.24">ver. 21-24</reference>. IV. The numbers, case, and peace, of his subjects, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.20-1Kgs.4.25">ver. 20-25</reference>. V. His stables, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.26">ver. 26</reference>. VI. His great reputation for wisdom and learning, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.29-1Kgs.4.34">ver. 29-34</reference>. Thus great was Solomon, but our Lord Jesus was greater than he (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">Matt. xii. 42</reference>), though he took upon him the form of a servant; for divinity, in its lowest humiliation, infinitely transcends royalty in its highest elevation.
entries.657d0d93defe38cd49fb89abf6f20daddee11bf4: <div eID="gen6578" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6577" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Officers. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1014.)</title> <div sID="gen6579" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So king Solomon was king over all Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And these <hi type="italic">were</hi> the princes which he had; Azariah the son of Zadok the priest, <hi type="super">3</hi> Elihoreph and Ahiah, the sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the host: and Zadok and Abiathar <hi type="italic">were</hi> the priests: <hi type="super">5</hi> And Azariah the son of Nathan <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan <hi type="italic">was</hi> principal officer, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the king's friend: <hi type="super">6</hi> And Ahishar <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the household: and Adoniram the son of Abda <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the tribute. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision. <hi type="super">8</hi> And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> their names: The son of Hur, in mount Ephraim: <hi type="super">9</hi> The son of Dekar, in Makaz, and in Shaalbim, and Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan: <hi type="super">10</hi> The son of Hesed, in Aruboth; to him <hi type="italic">pertained</hi> Sochoh, and all the land of Hepher: <hi type="super">11</hi> The son of Abinadab, in all the region of Dor; which had Taphath the daughter of Solomon to wife: <hi type="super">12</hi> Baana the son of Ahilud; <hi type="italic">to him pertained</hi> Taanach and Megiddo, and all Beth-shean, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by Zartanah beneath Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto <hi type="italic">the place that is</hi> beyond Jokneam: <hi type="super">13</hi> The son of Geber, in Ramoth-gilead; to him <hi type="italic">pertained</hi> the towns of Jair the son of Manasseh, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in Gilead; to him <hi type="italic">also pertained</hi> the region of Argob, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Bashan, threescore great cities with walls and brasen bars: <hi type="super">14</hi> Ahinadab the son of Iddo <hi type="italic">had</hi> Mahanaim: <hi type="super">15</hi> Ahimaaz <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Naphtali; he also took Basmath the daughter of Solomon to wife: <hi type="super">16</hi> Baanah the son of Hushai <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Asher and in Aloth: <hi type="super">17</hi> Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar: <hi type="super">18</hi> Shimei the son of Elah, in Benjamin: <hi type="super">19</hi> Geber the son of Uri <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the country of Gilead, <hi type="italic">in</hi> the country of Sihon king of the Amorites, and of Og king of Bashan; and <hi type="italic">he was</hi> the only officer which <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the land. <div eID="gen6579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6580" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen6580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6581" type="x-p"/> I. Solomon upon his throne (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">So king Solomon was king,</hi> that is, he was confirmed and established king <hi type="italic">over all Israel,</hi> and not, as his successors, only over two tribes. He was a king, that is, he did the work and duty of a king, with the wisdom God had given him. Those preserve the name and honour of their place that mind the business of it and make conscience of it. <div eID="gen6581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6582" type="x-p"/> II. The great officers of his court, in the choice of whom, no doubt, his wisdom much appeared. It is observable, 1. That several of them are the same that were in his father's time. Zadok and Abiathar were then priests (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2 Sam. xx. 25</reference>), so they were now; only then Abiathar had the precedency, now Zadok. Jehoshaphat was then recorder, or keeper of the great seal, so he was now. Benaiah, in his father's time, was a principal man in military affairs, and so he was now. Shisha was his father's scribe, and his sons were his, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.3">v. 3</reference>. Solomon, though a wise man, would not affect to be wiser than his father in this matter. When sons come to inherit their father's wealth, honour, and power, it is a piece of respect to their memory, <hi type="italic">cæteris paribus—where it can properly be done,</hi> to employ those whom they employed, and trust those whom they trusted. Many pride themselves in being the reverse of their good parents. 2. The rest were priests' sons. His prime-minister of state was <hi type="italic">Azariah the son of Zadok the priest.</hi> Two others of the first rank were the sons of Nathan the prophet, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.5">v. 5</reference>. In preferring them he testified the grateful respect he had for their good father, whom he loved <hi type="italic">in the name of a prophet.</hi> <div eID="gen6582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6583" type="x-p"/> III. The purveyors for his household, whose business it was to send in provisions from several parts of the country, for the king's tables and cellars (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.7">v. 7</reference>) and for his stables (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.27-1Kgs.4.28">v. 27, 28</reference>), that thus, 1. His house might always be well furnished at the best hand. Let great men learn hence good house-keeping, to be generous in spending according to their ability, but prudent in providing. It is the character of the virtuous woman that she <hi type="italic">bringeth her food from afar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.14">Prov. xxxi. 14</reference>), not far-fetched and dear-bought, but the contrary, every thing bought where it is cheapest. 2. That thus he himself, and those who immediately attended him, might be eased of a great deal of care, and the more closely apply themselves to the business of the state, not troubled about much serving, provision for that being got ready to their hand. 3. That thus all the parts of the kingdom might be equally benefited by the taking off of the commodities that were the productions of their country and the circulating of the coin. Industry would hereby be encouraged, and consequently wealth increased, even in those tribes that lay most remote from the court. The providence of God extends itself to all <hi type="italic">places of his dominions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.22">Ps. ciii. 22</reference>); so should the prudence and care of princes. 4. The dividing of this trust into so many hands was prudent, that no man might be continually burdened with the care of it nor grow exorbitantly rich with the profit of it, but that Solomon might have those, in every district, who, having a dependence upon the court, would be serviceable to him and his interest as there was occasion. These commissioners of the victualling-office, not for the army or navy (Solomon was engaged in no war), but for the household, are here named, several of them only by their surnames, as great men commonly call their servants: <hi type="italic">Ben-hur, Ben-dekar, &c.,</hi> though several of them have also their proper names prefixed. Two of them married Solomon's daughters, Ben-Abinadab (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.11">v. 11</reference>) and Ahimaaz (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.15">v. 15</reference>), and no disparagement to them to marry men of business. Better match with the officers of their father's court that were Israelites than with the sons of princes that were <hi type="italic">strangers to the covenant of promise.</hi> The son of Geber was in Ramoth-Gilead (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.19">v. 19</reference>), and Geber himself was in the country of Sihon and Og, which included that and Mahanaim, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.14">v. 14</reference>. He is therefore said to be <hi type="italic">the only officer in that land,</hi> because the other two, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.13-1Kgs.4.14">v. 13, 14</reference>, depended on him, and were subordinate to him.
entries.b61a17bad9870dd7667179734f3c0f4cfc178160: <div eID="gen6583" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Supply of Solomon's Household. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1014.)</title> <div sID="gen6584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> Judah and Israel <hi type="italic">were</hi> many, as the sand which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the sea in multitude, eating and drinking, and making merry. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Solomon reigned over all kingdoms from the river unto the land of the Philistines, and unto the border of Egypt: they brought presents, and served Solomon all the days of his life. <hi type="super">22</hi> And Solomon's provision for one day was thirty measures of fine flour, and threescore measures of meal, <hi type="super">23</hi> Ten fat oxen, and twenty oxen out of the pastures, and an hundred sheep, beside harts, and roebucks, and fallowdeer, and fatted fowl. <hi type="super">24</hi> For he had dominion over all <hi type="italic">the region</hi> on this side the river, from Tiphsah even to Azzah, over all the kings on this side the river: and he had peace on all sides round about him. <hi type="super">25</hi> And Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beer-sheba, all the days of Solomon. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses for his chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen. <hi type="super">27</hi> And those officers provided victual for king Solomon, and for all that came unto king Solomon's table, every man in his month: they lacked nothing. <hi type="super">28</hi> Barley also and straw for the horses and dromedaries brought they unto the place where <hi type="italic">the officers</hi> were, every man according to his charge. <div eID="gen6584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6585" type="x-p"/> Such a kingdom, and such a court, surely never any prince had, as Solomon's are here described to be. <div eID="gen6585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6586" type="x-p"/> I. Such a kingdom. Never did the crown of Israel shine so brightly as it did when Solomon wore it, never in his father's days, never in the days of any of his successors; nor was that kingdom ever so glorious a type of the kingdom of the Messiah as it was then. The account here given of it is such as fully answers the prophecies which we have concerning it in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1-Ps.72.20">Ps. lxxii.</reference>, which is a psalm for Solomon, but with reference to Christ. 1. The territories of his kingdom were large and its tributaries many; so it was foretold that he should <hi type="italic">have dominion from sea to sea,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8-Ps.72.11">Ps. lxxii. 8-11</reference>. Solomon reigned not only over all Israel, who were his subjects by choice, but over all the neighbouring kingdoms, who were his subjects by constraint. All the princes from the river Euphrates, north-east to the border of Egypt south-west, not only added to his honour by doing him homage and holding their crowns from him, but added to his wealth by serving him, and bringing him presents, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">v. 21</reference>. David, by his successful wars, compelled them to this subjection, and Solomon, by his admirable wisdom, made it easy and reasonable; for it is fit that the fool should be <hi type="italic">servant to the wise in heart.</hi> If they gave him presents, he gave them instructions, and still <hi type="italic">taught the people knowledge,</hi> not only his own people, but those of other nations: and <hi type="italic">wisdom is better than gold.</hi> He had <hi type="italic">peace on all sides,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.24">v. 24</reference>. None of all the nations that were subject to him offered to shake off his yoke, or to give him any disturbance, but rather thought themselves happy in their dependence upon him. Herein his kingdom typified the Messiah's; for to him it is promised that he shall have the <hi type="italic">heathen for his inheritance</hi> and that <hi type="italic">princes shall worship him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6-Isa.49.7">Isa. xlix. 6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">liii. 12</reference>. 2. The subjects of his kingdom and its inhabitants, were many and cheerful. (1.) They were numerous and country was exceedingly populous (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judah and Israel were many,</hi> and that good land was sufficient to maintain them all. <hi type="italic">They were as the sand of the sea in multitude.</hi> Now was fulfilled the promise made to Abraham concerning the increase of his seed (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen. xxii. 17</reference>), as well as that concerning the extent of their dominion, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen. xv. 18</reference>. This was their strength and beauty, the honour of their prince, the terror of their enemies, and an advancement of the wealth of the nation. If they grew so numerous that the place was any where too strait for them, they might remove with advantage into the countries that were subject to them. God's spiritual Israel are many, at least they will be so when they come all together, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev. vii. 9</reference>. (2.) They were easy, they dwelt safely, or with confidence and assurance (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">v. 25</reference>), not jealous of their king or of his officers, not disaffected either to him or one to another, nor under any apprehension or danger from enemies foreign or domestic. They were happy and knew it, safe and willing to think themselves so. They dwelt every man under <hi type="italic">his vine and fig-tree.</hi> Solomon invaded no man's property, took not to himself their vineyards and olive-yards, as sometimes was the manner of the king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.14">1 Sam. viii. 14</reference>), but what they had they could call their own: he protected every man in the possession and enjoyment of his property. Those that had vines and fig-trees ate the fruit of them themselves; and so great was the peace of the country that they might, if they pleased, dwell as safely under the shadow of them as within the walls of a city. Or, because it was usual to have <hi type="italic">vines by the sides of their houses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">Ps. cxxviii. 3</reference>), they are said to <hi type="italic">dwell under their vines.</hi> (3.) They were cheerful in the use of their plenty, <hi type="italic">eating and drinking, and making merry,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.20">v. 20</reference>. Solomon did not only keep a good table himself, but enabled all his subjects, according to their rank, to do so too, and taught them that God gave them their abundance that they might use it soberly and pleasantly, not that they might hoard it up. <hi type="italic">There is nothing better</hi> than for a man to <hi type="italic">eat the labour of his hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Eccl. ii. 24</reference>), and that <hi type="italic">with a merry heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7">Eccl. ix. 7</reference>. His father, in the Psalms, had led his people into the comforts of communion with God, and now he led them into the comfortable use of the good things of this life. This pleasant posture of Israel's affairs extended, in place, from Dan to Beer-sheba—no part of the country was exposed nor upon any account uneasy; and it continued a long time, <hi type="italic">all the days of Solomon,</hi> without any material interruption. Go where you would, you might see all the marks of plenty, peace, and satisfaction. The spiritual peace, and joy, and holy security, of all the faithful subjects of the Lord Jesus were typified by this. <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God is not,</hi> as Solomon's was, <hi type="italic">meat and drink,</hi> but, what is infinitely better, <hi type="italic">righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.</hi> <div eID="gen6586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6587" type="x-p"/> II. Such a court Solomon kept as can scarcely be paralleled. We may guess at the vast number of his attendants, and the great resort there was to him, by the provision that was made daily for his table. Of bread there were so many measures of flour and meal as, it is computed, would richly serve 3000 men (Carellus computes above 4800 men), and the provision of flesh (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.23">v. 23</reference>) was rather more in proportion. What vast quantities were here of beef, mutton, and venison, and the choicest of all <hi type="italic">fatted things,</hi> as some read that which we translate <hi type="italic">fatted fowl!</hi> Ahasuerus, once in his reign, made a <hi type="italic">great feast,</hi> to <hi type="italic">show the riches of his kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.1.3-Esth.1.4">Esth. i. 3, 4</reference>. But it was much more the honour of Solomon that he kept a constant table and a very noble one, not of dainties or deceitful meats (he himself witnessed against them, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Prov. xxiii. 3</reference>), but substantial food, for the entertainment of those who came to hear his wisdom. Thus Christ fed those whom he taught, 5000 at a time, more than ever Solomon's table would entertain at once: and all believers have in him a continual feast. Herein he far outdoes Solomon, that he feeds all his subjects, not with the bread that perishes, but <hi type="italic">with that which endures to eternal life.</hi> It added much both to the strength and glory of Solomon's kingdom that he had such abundance of horses, 40,000 for chariots and 12,000 for his troops, 1000 horse, perhaps, in every tribe, for the preserving of the public peace, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.26">v. 26</reference>. God had commanded that their king should not multiply horses (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">Deut. xvii. 16</reference>), nor, according to the account here given, considering the extent and wealth of Solomon's kingdom, did he multiply horses in proportion to his neighbours; for we find even the Philistines bringing into the field 30,000 chariots (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.5">1 Sam. xiii. 5</reference>) and the Syrians at least 40,000 horse, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2 Sam. x. 18</reference>. The same officers that provided for his house provided also for his stable, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.27-1Kgs.4.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. Every one knew his place, and work, and time; and so this great court was kept without confusion. Solomon, that had vast incomes, lived at a vast expense, and perhaps wrote that with application to himself, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Eccl. v. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">When goods increase those are increased that eat them; and what good is there to the owners thereof, saving the beholding of them with their eyes,</hi> unless withal they have the satisfaction of doing good with them?
entries.e7419e389eeeb034976d0382284adb83f25b4759: <div eID="gen6587" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Distinguished Reputation. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1014.)</title> <div sID="gen6588" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the sea shore. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Solomon's wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east country, and all the wisdom of Egypt. <hi type="super">31</hi> For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol: and his fame was in all nations round about. <hi type="super">32</hi> And he spake three thousand proverbs: and his songs were a thousand and five. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he spake of trees, from the cedar tree that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that springeth out of the wall: he spake also of beasts, and of fowl, and of creeping things, and of fishes. <hi type="super">34</hi> And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon, from all kings of the earth, which had heard of his wisdom. <div eID="gen6588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6589" type="x-p"/> Solomon's wisdom was more his glory than his wealth, and here we have a general account of it. <div eID="gen6589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6590" type="x-p"/> I. The fountain of his wisdom: <hi type="italic">God gave it him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.29">v. 29</reference>. He owns it himself. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Prov. ii. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord giveth wisdom.</hi> He gives the powers of reason (<reference osisRef="Job.38.36">Job xxxviii. 36</reference>), preserves and improves them. The ordinary advances of them are owing to his providence, the sanctification of them to his grace, and this extraordinary pitch at which they arrived in Solomon to a special grant of his favour to him in answer to prayer. <div eID="gen6590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6591" type="x-p"/> II. The fulness of it: <hi type="italic">He had wisdom and understanding, exceeding much,</hi> great knowledge of distant countries and the histories of former times, a quickness of thought, strength of memory, and clearness of judgment, such as never any man had. It is called <hi type="italic">largeness of heart;</hi> for the heart is often put for the intellectual powers. He had a vast compass of knowledge, could take things entire, and had an admirable faculty of laying things together. Some, by his <hi type="italic">largeness of heart,</hi> understand his courage and boldness, and that great assurance with which he delivered his dictates and determinations. Or it may be meant of his disposition to do good with his knowledge. He was very free and communicative, had the gift of utterance as well as wisdom, was as free of his learning as he was of his meat, and grudged neither to any that were about him. Note, It is very desirable that those who have large gifts of any kind should have large hearts to use them for the good of others; and this is <hi type="italic">from the hand of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Eccl. ii. 24</reference>. He shall <hi type="italic">enlarge the heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.32">Ps. cxix. 32</reference>. The greatness of Solomon's wisdom is illustrated by comparison. Chaldea and Egypt were nations famous for learning; thence the Greeks borrowed theirs; but the greatest scholars of these nations came short of Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.30">v. 30</reference>. If nature excels art, much more does grace. The knowledge which God gives by special favour goes beyond that which man gets by his own labour. Some wise men there were in Solomon's time, who were in great repute, particularly Heman, and others who were Levites, and employed by David in the temple-music, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1 Chron. xv. 19</reference>. Heman was <hi type="italic">his seer in the word of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.5">1 Chron. xxv. 5</reference>. Chalcol and Darda were own brothers, and they also were noted for learning and wisdom. But <hi type="italic">Solomon excelled them all</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.30">v. 30</reference>), he out-did them and confounded them; his counsel was much more valuable. <div eID="gen6591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6592" type="x-p"/> III. The fame of it. It was talked of <hi type="italic">in all nations round about.</hi> His great wealth and glory made his wisdom much more illustrious, and have him those opportunities of showing it which those cannot have that live in poverty and obscurity. The jewel of wisdom may receive great advantage by the setting of it. <div eID="gen6592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6593" type="x-p"/> IV. The fruits of it; by these the tree is known: he did not bury his talent, but showed his wisdom, <div eID="gen6593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6594" type="x-p"/> 1. In his compositions. Those in divinity, written by divine inspiration, are not mentioned here, for they are extant, and will remain to the world's end monuments of his wisdom, and are, as other parts of scripture, of use to make us <hi type="italic">wise unto salvation.</hi> But, besides these, it appears by what he spoke, or dictated to be written from him, (1.) That he was a moralist, and a man of great prudence, for he spoke 3000 <hi type="italic">proverbs,</hi> wise sayings, apophthegms, of admirable use for the conduct of human life. The world is much governed by proverbs, and was never better furnished with useful ones than by Solomon. Whether those proverbs of Solomon that we have were any part of the 3000 is uncertain. (2.) That he was a poet and a man of great wit: <hi type="italic">His songs were</hi> 1005, of which one only is extant, because that only was divinely inspired, which is therefore called his <hi type="italic">Song of songs.</hi> His wise instructions were communicated by proverbs, that they might be familiar to those whom he designed to teach and ready on all occasions, and by <hi type="italic">songs,</hi> that they might be pleasant and move the affections. (3.) That he was a natural philosopher, and a man of great learning and insight into the mysteries of nature. From his own and others' observations and experience, he wrote both of plants and animals (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">v. 33</reference>), descriptions of their natures and qualities, and (some think) of the medicinal use of them. <div eID="gen6594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6595" type="x-p"/> 2. In his conversation. There came persons from all parts, who were more inquisitive after knowledge than their neighbours, to <hi type="italic">hear the wisdom of Solomon,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.34">v. 34</reference>. Kings that had heard of it sent their ambassadors to hear it and to bring them instructions from it. Solomon's court was the staple of learning, and the rendezvous of philosophers, that is, the lovers of wisdom, who all came to light their candle at his lamp and to borrow from him. Let those who magnify the modern learning above that of the ancients produce such a treasure of knowledge any where in these latter ages as that was which Solomon was master of; yet this puts an honour upon human learning, that Solomon was praised for it, and recommends it to the great men of the earth, as well worthy their diligent search. But, <div eID="gen6595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Solomon was, herein, a type of Christ, <hi type="italic">in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,</hi> and hidden for use; for he is <hi type="italic">made of God to us wisdom.</hi>  <chapter eID="1Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen6596" type="x-p"/>

entries.a69ed589de0ae58b998f195be1aec78a5c124dca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3112"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen4327" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.1-1Kgs.4.6">1Ki 4:1-6</reference>. Solomon's Princes.<div eID="gen4327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3112"/><hi type="bold">1. So King Solomon was king over all Israel--</hi>This chapter contains a general description of the state and glory of the Hebrew kingdom during the more flourishing or later years of his reign. <div eID="gen4328" type="x-p"/>
entries.f438b9bfb0529aa1e4ec5b723ffb72446baa4950: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3113"/><div sID="gen4329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3113"/><hi type="bold">2. these were the princes--</hi>or chief officers, as is evident from two of them marrying Solomon's daughters.<div eID="gen4329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Azariah the son of Zadok the priest--</hi>rather, "the prince," as the Hebrew word frequently signifies (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Ge 41:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.2.16">Ex 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference>); so that from the precedency given to his person in the list, he seems to have been prime minister, the highest in office next the king. <div eID="gen4330" type="x-p"/>
entries.e79aadd58c0c380e234b621bedd1da0ea6107a62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3114"/><div sID="gen4331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3114"/><hi type="bold">3. scribes--</hi>that is, secretaries of state. Under David, there had been only one [2Sa 8:17; 20:25]. The employment of three functionaries in this department indicates either improved regulations by the division of labor, or a great increase of business, occasioned by the growing prosperity of the kingdom, or a more extensive correspondence with foreign countries.<div eID="gen4331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">recorder--</hi>that is, historiographer, or annalist--an office of great importance in Oriental courts, and the duties of which consisted in chronicling the occurrences of every day. <div eID="gen4332" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed20db45c4227eb0c8503a231190ff5ea26cc678: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3115"/><div sID="gen4333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3115"/><hi type="bold">4. Benaiah ... was over the host--</hi>formerly captain of the guard. He had succeeded Joab as commander of the forces.<div eID="gen4333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zadok and Abiathar were the priests--</hi>Only the first discharged the sacred functions; the latter had been banished to his country seat and retained nothing more than the name of high priest. <div eID="gen4334" type="x-p"/>
entries.60534494b0460b8bfabe9c7b1021f704e535ad58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3116"/><div sID="gen4335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3116"/><hi type="bold">5. over the officers--</hi>that is, the provincial governors enumerated in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.17-1Kgs.4.19">1Ki 4:17-19</reference>.<div eID="gen4335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">principal officer, and the king's friend--</hi>perhaps president of the privy council, and Solomon's confidential friend or favorite. This high functionary had probably been reared along with Solomon. That he should heap those honors on the sons of Nathan was most natural, considering the close intimacy of the father with the late king, and the deep obligations under which Solomon personally lay to the prophet. <div eID="gen4336" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfa676b2fc09e888d1106fcae704404a40d87023: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3117"/><div sID="gen4337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3117"/><hi type="bold">6. Ahishar was over the household--</hi>steward or chamberlain of the palace.<div eID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Adoniram--</hi>or Adoram (<reference osisRef="2Sam.20.24">2Sa 20:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.18">1Ki 12:18</reference>), or Hadoram (<reference osisRef="2Chr.10.18">2Ch 10:18</reference>),<div eID="gen4338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was over the tribute--</hi>not the collection of money or goods, but the levy of compulsory laborers (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.13">1Ki 5:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4340" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.7-1Kgs.4.21">1Ki 4:7-21</reference>. His Twelve Officers. <div eID="gen4340" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9f3b01fcd1c063fc72c02962d43588cfaa53f84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3118"/><div sID="gen4341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3118"/><hi type="bold">7. Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel--</hi>The royal revenues were raised according to the ancient, and still, in many parts, existing usage of the East, not in money payments, but in the produce of the soil. There would be always a considerable difficulty in the collection and transmission of these tithes (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.15">1Sa 8:15</reference>). Therefore, to facilitate the work, Solomon appointed twelve officers, who had each the charge of a tribe or particular district of country, from which, in monthly rotation, the supplies for the maintenance of the king's household were drawn, having first been deposited in "the store cities" which were erected for their reception (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.19">1Ki 9:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.4">2Ch 8:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen4341" type="x-p"/>
entries.dba303f0d4680c1bdbabef9eb81dd274d7597bb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3119"/><div sID="gen4342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3119"/><hi type="bold">8. The son of Hur--</hi>or, as the Margin has it, Benhur, Bendekar. In the rural parts of Syria, and among the Arabs, it is still common to designate persons not by their own names, but as the sons of their fathers. <div eID="gen4342" type="x-p"/>
entries.14e88c5cc09d8e698c2f95fec5013a25f212d5af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3120"/><div sID="gen4343" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3120"/><hi type="bold">21. Solomon reigned over all kingdoms from the river--</hi>All the petty kingdoms between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean were tributary to him. Similar is the statement in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.24">1Ki 4:24</reference>. <div eID="gen4343" type="x-p"/>
entries.444161f1d59fc9da5469cce5af8399a8edd84d88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3121"/><div sID="gen4344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3121"/><hi type="bold">22-23. Solomon's provision for one day--</hi>not for the king's table only, but for all connected with the court, including, besides the royal establishment, those of his royal consorts, his principal officers, his bodyguards, his foreign visitors, &c. The quantity of fine floor used is estimated at two hundred forty bushels; that of meal or common flour at four hundred eighty. The number of cattle required for consumption, besides poultry and several kinds of game (which were abundant on the mountains) did not exceed in proportion what is needed in other courts of the East. <div eID="gen4344" type="x-p"/>
entries.6301b4d0225937056e5559db1259d4b31c139db3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3122"/><div sID="gen4345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3122"/><hi type="bold">24. from Tiphsah--</hi>that is, Thapsacus, a large and flourishing town on the west bank of the Euphrates, the name of which was derived from a celebrated ford near it, the lowest on that river.<div eID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even to Azzah--</hi>that is, Gaza, on the southwestern extremity, not far from the Mediterranean. <div eID="gen4346" type="x-p"/>
entries.38570fa7d3137942182837889c66dfbf6dc0f134: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3123"/><div sID="gen4347" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3123"/><hi type="bold">25. every man under his vine and ... fig tree--</hi>This is a common and beautiful metaphor for peace and security (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.4">Mi 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.10">Zec 3:10</reference>), founded on the practice, still common in modern Syria, of training these fruit trees up the walls and stairs of houses, so as to make a shady arbor, beneath which the people sit and relax. <div eID="gen4347" type="x-p"/>
entries.85bdde91712cfe7ccca76950c9d1face7165cc9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3124"/><div sID="gen4348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3124"/><hi type="bold">26. forty thousand stalls--</hi>for the royal mews (see on <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.25">2Ch 9:25</reference>). <div eID="gen4348" type="x-p"/>
entries.36c31b3a2bf17fccd1f587618f896059a49615dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3125"/><div sID="gen4349" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3125"/><hi type="bold">28. Barley ... and straw--</hi>Straw is not used for litter, but barley mixed with chopped straw is the usual fodder of horses.<div eID="gen4349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dromedaries--</hi>one-humped camels, distinguished for their great fleetness.<div eID="gen4350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.29-1Kgs.4.34">1Ki 4:29-34</reference>. His Wisdom. <div eID="gen4351" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3758aacdc9b2f9277deaee22799bcb3c697a7cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3126"/><div sID="gen4352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3126"/><hi type="bold">29. God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart--</hi>that is, high powers of mind, great capacity for receieving, as well as aptitude for communicating knowledge. <div eID="gen4352" type="x-p"/>
entries.84ee88c8883e4f1d097cacb56e6cecc91917db39: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3127"/><div sID="gen4353" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3127"/><hi type="bold">30. Solomon's wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east country--</hi>that is, the Arabians, Chaldeans, and Persians (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.6">Ge 25:6</reference>).<div eID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the wisdom of Egypt--</hi>Egypt was renowned as the seat of learning and sciences, and the existing monuments, which so clearly describe the ancient state of society and the arts, show the high culture of the Egyptian people. <div eID="gen4354" type="x-p"/>
entries.f513507a41b570553962d321dbd21162702621b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3128"/><div sID="gen4355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3128"/><hi type="bold">31. wiser than all men--</hi>that is, all his contemporaries, either at home or abroad.<div eID="gen4355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than Ethan--</hi>or Jeduthun, of the family of Merari (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.44">1Ch 6:44</reference>).<div eID="gen4356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Heman--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.17-1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:17-19</reference>)--the chief of the temple musicians and the king's seers (<reference osisRef="1Chr.25.5">1Ch 25:5</reference>); the other two are not known.<div eID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4358" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sons of Mahol--</hi>either another name for Zerah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.6">1Ch 2:6</reference>); or taking it as a common noun, signifying a dance, a chorus, "the sons of Mahol" signify persons eminently skilled in poetry and music. <div eID="gen4358" type="x-p"/>
entries.19bc682dc08dede740a16f61727dd8f90baafc62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3129"/><div sID="gen4359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3129"/><hi type="bold">32. he spake three thousand proverbs--</hi>embodying his moral sentiments and sage observations on human life and character.<div eID="gen4359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">songs ... a thousand and five--</hi>Psalm 72, 127, 132, and the Song of Songs are his. <div eID="gen4360" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbb14c57634e9972636aee651fc2d1ea71d6283d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3130"/><div sID="gen4361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3130"/><hi type="bold">33. he spake of trees, from the cedar ... to the hyssop--</hi>all plants, from the greatest to the least. The Spirit of God has seen fit to preserve comparatively few memorials of the fruits of his gigantic mind. The greater part of those here ascribed to him have long since fallen a prey to the ravages of time, or perished in the Babylonish captivity, probably because they were not inspired. <chapter eID="1Kgs.4"/>

entries.b29c5e5ef59d4e5d6670132a96690509b31bb32c: <div eID="gen11571" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11572" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11573" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11573" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11572" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11574" type="x-p"/> An account of Solomon's chief officers, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.1-1Kgs.4.6">1Kgs 4:1-6</reference>. Names of the twelve officers that were over twelve districts, to provide victuals for the king's household monthly, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.7-1Kgs.4.19">1Kgs 4:7-19</reference>. Judah and Israel are very populous; and Solomon reigns over many provinces, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.20">1Kgs 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.21">1Kgs 4:21</reference>. The daily provision for his family, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.22">1Kgs 4:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.23">1Kgs 4:23</reference>. The extent and peace of his dominions, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.24">1Kgs 4:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">1Kgs 4:25</reference>. His horses, chariots, and dromedaries; with the provision made for them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.26-1Kgs.4.28">1Kgs 4:26-28</reference>. His wisdom and understanding, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.29-1Kgs.4.31">1Kgs 4:29-31</reference>. The number of his proverbs and songs; and his knowledge in natural history, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.32">1Kgs 4:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">1Kgs 4:33</reference>. People from all nations come to hear his wisdom, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.34">1Kgs 4:34</reference>.
entries.ab4e08cbeaf3d73733c44349d198fd5a6bcc4664: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen11574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11575" type="x-p"/> These were the princes which he had; Azariah the son of Zadok the priest - These were his great, chief, or principal men. None of them were princes in the common acceptation of the word.
entries.53a0cad70925afff04c590b43cd4b8fb01cfdb6e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11576" type="x-p"/> Elihoreph and Ahiah - scribes - Secretaries to the king. <div eID="gen11576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11577" type="x-p"/> Jehoshaphat - recorder - Historiographer to the king, who chronicled the affairs of the kingdom. He was in this office under David see <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.24">2Sam 20:24</reference>.
entries.b4d6aca8f34e336b94dd49cea062c29762c440ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11578" type="x-p"/> Azariah - was over the officers - He had the superintendence of the twelve officers mentioned below; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.7">1Kgs 4:7</reference>. <div eID="gen11578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11579" type="x-p"/> Zabud - was principal officer - Perhaps what we call premier, or prime minister. <div eID="gen11579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11580" type="x-p"/> The king's friend - His chief favourite - his confidant.
entries.fc2f93aae699240ac01a01cf1841496e905ef24a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen11580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11581" type="x-p"/> Ahishar was over the household - The king's chamberlain. <div eID="gen11581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11582" type="x-p"/> Adoniram - was over the tribute - What we call chancellor of the exchequer. He received and brought into the treasury all the proceeds of taxes and tributes. He was in this office under David; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.24">2Sam 20:24</reference>.
entries.356579e0d83d5953fa1385eca4f2aad8b25768bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen11582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11583" type="x-p"/> Twelve officers - The business of these twelve officers was to provide daily, each for a month, those provisions which were consumed in the king's household; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.22">1Kgs 4:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.23">1Kgs 4:23</reference>. And the task for such a daily provision was not an easy one.
entries.e06348f335e193f46b5a3d536174d272a51f4aa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen11583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11584" type="x-p"/> Threescore great cities with walls and brazen bars - These were fortified cities: their gates and bars covered with plates of brass. Such were the gates in Priam's palace: - <div eID="gen11584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11585" type="x-p"/> Ipse inter primos correpta dura bipenni <div eID="gen11585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11586" type="x-p"/> Limina perrumpit, Postes que a cardine vellit <div eID="gen11586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11587" type="x-p"/> Aeratos. Virg. Aen., lib. ii. ver. 479. <div eID="gen11587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11588" type="x-p"/> Fierce Pyrrhus in the front, with forceful sway, <div eID="gen11588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11589" type="x-p"/> Plied the huge axe, and hew'd the beams away; <div eID="gen11589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11590" type="x-p"/> The solid timbers from the portal tore, <div eID="gen11590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11591" type="x-p"/> And rent from every hinge the Brazen door. <div eID="gen11591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11592" type="x-p"/> Pitt.
entries.1329dab18024a0be6c7072d595c974f4fcde0f5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen11592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11593" type="x-p"/> Eating and drinking, and making merry - They were very comfortable, very rich, very merry, and very corrupt. And this full feeding and dissipation led to a total corruption of manners.
entries.ae776caa66f16d310455746040ae4b7a26c18c76: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen11593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11594" type="x-p"/> Solomon reigned over all kingdoms - The meaning of this verse appears to be, that Solomon reigned over all the provinces from the river Euphrates to the land of the Philistines, even to the frontiers of Egypt. The Euphrates was on the east of Solomon's dominions; the Philistines were westward on the Mediterranean sea; and Egypt was on the south. Solomon had, therefore, as tributaries, the kingdoms of Syria, Damascus, Moab, and Ammon, which lay between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean. See Calmet. Thus he appears to have possessed all the land that God covenanted with Abraham to give to his posterity.
entries.6bb3607f3cf22ab8fa358a14b14eab58ba4e7d2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen11594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11595" type="x-p"/> Solomon's provision for one day: - <div eID="gen11595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11596" type="x-p"/> Of fine flour 30 measures, or cors. Of meal 60 ditto. Stall-fed oxen 10 Ditto from the pasture 20 Sheep 100; with harts, roebucks, fallow deer, and fat fowls. The כר cor was the same as the homer, and contained nearly seventy-six gallons, wine measure, according to Bishop Cumberland. <div eID="gen11596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11597" type="x-p"/> Sheep - צאן tson, comprehending both sheep and goats. <div eID="gen11597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11598" type="x-p"/> Harts - מאיל meaiyal, the deer. <div eID="gen11598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11599" type="x-p"/> Roebucks - צבי tsebi, the gazal, antelope, or wild goat. <div eID="gen11599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11600" type="x-p"/> Fallow deer - יחמור yachmur, the buffalo. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Deu.12.15">Deu 12:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.14.5">Deu 14:5</reference>. <div eID="gen11600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11601" type="x-p"/> Fatted fowl - ברברים אבוסים barburim abusim, I suppose, means all the wild fowls in season during each month. Michaelis derives ברברים barburim from ברא bara, which in Chaldee, Syriac, and Arabic, signifies a field, a desert; all that is without the cities and habitations of men: hence חיות ברא cheyvath bara, wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Dan 2:38</reference>, תור בר tor bar, wild bull; and therefore barburim may signify creatures living in the fields, woods, and deserts, which are taken by hunting, and opposed to those which are domesticated; and, consequently, may include beasts as well as fowls. Many have translated the word capons; but, query, was any such thing known among the ancient Jews? Solomon's table, therefore, was spread with all the necessaries and delicacies which the house or the field could afford. <div eID="gen11601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11602" type="x-p"/> But how immense must the number of men have been who were fed daily at the palace of the Israelitish king! Vilalpandus computes the number to be not less than forty-eight thousand, six hundred; and Calvisius makes, by estimation from the consumption of food, fifty-four thousand! These must have included all his guards, each of whom received a ration from the king's store.
entries.ae3af0b3b5bbe5eceea3b46a6c107c61bd6624d4: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen11602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11603" type="x-p"/> Every man under his vine - They were no longer obliged to dwell in fortified cities for fear of their enemies; they spread themselves over all the country, which they everywhere cultivated; and had always the privilege of eating the fruits of their own labors. This is the meaning of the phrase.
entries.065f35cd88b123e6bc29583fbdaaaf68bc8a7f30: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen11603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11604" type="x-p"/> Solomon had forty thousand stalls of horses - and twelve thousand horsemen - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.25">2Chr 9:25</reference>, instead of forty thousand stalls, we read four thousand; and even this number might be quite sufficient to hold horses for twelve thousand horsemen; for stalls and stables may be here synonymous. In <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.26">1Kgs 10:26</reference> it is said he had one thousand four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen; and this is the reading in <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.14">2Chr 1:14</reference>. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.25">2Chr 9:25</reference>, already quoted, instead of forty thousand stalls for horses, the Septuagint has τεσσαρες χιλιαδες θηλειαι ἱπποι, four thousand mares; and in this place the whole verse is omitted both by the Syriac and Arabic. In the Targum of Rabbi Joseph on this book we have ארבע מאה arba meah, four hundred, instead of the four thousand in Chronicles, and the forty thousand in the text. From this collation of parallel places we may rest satisfied that there is a corruption in the numbers somewhere; and as a sort of medium, we may take for the whole four thousand stalls, one thousand four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen.
entries.000a4be0f91ced2505c4c012bc1b09c6832064fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen11604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11605" type="x-p"/> And dromedaries - The word רכש rechesh, which we translate thus, is rendered beasts, or beasts of burden, by the Vulgate; mares by the Syriac and Arabic; chariots by the Septuagint; and race-horses by the Chaldee. The original word seems to signify a very swift kind of horse, and race-horse or post-horse is probably its true meaning. To communicate with so many distant provinces, Solomon had need of many animals of this kind.
entries.5c2b64a06e006944b430aff5d77587dbdc4ddb0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen11605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11606" type="x-p"/> God gave Solomon wisdom, etc. - He gave him a capacious mind, and furnished him with extraordinary assistance to cultivate it. <div eID="gen11606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11607" type="x-p"/> Even as the sand that is on the sea-shore - Lord Bacon observes on this: "As the sand on the sea-shore encloses a great body of waters, so Solomon's mind contained an ocean of knowledge." This is a happy and correct illustration.
entries.b769b9f9cff2c8a9299823d9c4eabef6eed1183f: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen11607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11608" type="x-p"/> The children of the east country - That is the Chaldeans, Persians, and Arabians, who, with the Egyptians, were famed for wisdom and knowledge through all the world.
entries.5e7deb248f477c01dd0494df6d4a2ea652ded213: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen11608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11609" type="x-p"/> He was wiser than all men - He was wiser than any of those who were most celebrated in his time, among whom were the four after mentioned, viz., Ethan, Heman, Chalcol, and Darda. Ethan was probably the same as is mentioned in some of the Psalms, particularly <reference osisRef="Psa.89.1">Psa 89:1</reference>, title; and among the singers in <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.42">1Chr 6:42</reference>. There is a Heman mentioned in the title to <reference osisRef="Psa.88.1">Psa 88:1</reference>. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.6">1Chr 2:6</reference> we have all the four names, but they are probably not the same persons, for they are there said to be the sons of Zerah, and he flourished long before Solomon's time. <div eID="gen11609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11610" type="x-p"/> Some suppose that בני מחול beney machol should be rendered masters of dancing or music, as מחול machol signifies not only a dance or choir, but also an instrument of music of the pipe kind. Perhaps a reference is here made to Solomon's skill in music and poetry, as he is compared to persons who appear to have been eminent poets and musicians.
entries.a5ffa0a0c3ddd64e76bc826ac7b5b278a1c32ddf: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen11610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11611" type="x-p"/> He spake three thousand proverbs - The book of Proverbs, attributed to Solomon, contain only about nine hundred or nine hundred and twenty-three distinct proverbs; and if we grant with some that the first nine chapters are not the work of Solomon, then all that can be attributed to him is only about six hundred and fifty. <div eID="gen11611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11612" type="x-p"/> Of all his one thousand and five songs or poems we have only one, the book of Song of Solomon, remaining, unless we include <reference osisRef="Psa.127.1-Psa.127.5">Psa 127:1-5</reference>, Except the Lord build the house, etc., which in the title is said to be by or for him, though it appears more properly to be a psalm of direction, left him by his father David, relative to the building of the temple.
entries.88899139e92e5e346b17305145a0b2d6891844ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen11612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11613" type="x-p"/> He spake of trees - beasts - fowl - creeping things, and of fishes - This is a complete system of natural history, as far as relates to the animal and vegetable kingdoms, and the first intimation we have of any thing of the kind: Solomon was probably the first natural historian in the world. <div eID="gen11613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11614" type="x-p"/> O, how must the heart of Tournefort, Ray, Linne, Buffon, Cuvier, Swammerdam, Blosch, and other naturalists, be wrung, to know that these works of Solomon are all and for ever lost! What light should we have thrown on the animal and vegetable kingdoms, had these works been preserved! But the providence of God has not thought fit to preserve them, and succeeding naturalists are left to invent the system which he probably left perfect. If there be any remains of his wisdom, they must be sought among the orientals, among whom his character is well known, and rates as high as it does with either Jews or Christians. I shall give some extracts from their works relative to Solomon when I come to consider his character at the end of <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.43">1Kgs 11:43</reference>.
entries.916a711e07ef0664d078d6ff8e98ba0c1105437a: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen11614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11615" type="x-p"/> There came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon - We learn from 1 Kings 10, that the queen of Sheba was one of those visitants, and perhaps the most remarkable, as we have the particulars of her visit, but not of the others. <div eID="gen11615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11616" type="x-p"/> It is astonishing that of a person so renowned for wisdom, so little should be left to prove the truth of a fact of which all the civilized nations of the world have heard, and of which scarcely any man has ever doubted. The people that came from all kings of the earth were probably ambassadors, who came to form and maintain friendship between their sovereigns and the Israelitish king. We cannot understand the place as speaking of people who, either through an idle or laudable curiosity, came to see and converse with Solomon; to give free access to such people would ill comport with the maintenance of his dignity.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen11616" type="x-p"/>

entries.12d97ce338d668c8cf0c25f442aad1895801baa0: <div eID="gen4771" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Solomon’s Ministers of State. His Regal Splendour and Wisdom</title> <div sID="gen4772" type="x-p"/> 1 Kings 4 contains a list of the chief ministers of state (1Ki 4:2-6), and of the twelve officers placed over the land (1Ki 4:7-20), which is inserted here to give an idea of the might and glory of the kingdom of Israel under Solomon’s reign. So far as the contents are concerned, this list belongs to the middle portion of the reign of Solomon, as we may see from the fact that two of the officers named had daughters of Solomon for their wives (1Ki 4:11, 1Ki 4:15), whom they could not possibly have married till the later years of Solomon’s life. <div eID="gen4772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4773" type="x-p"/> The Chief Ministers of State. - The list is introduced in 1Ki 4:1 by the general remark, that “king Solomon was king over all Israel.”
entries.a1b8a6ecf071337b16c06e761fb3eee280be3de0: 1Ki 4:2 <div eID="gen4773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4774" type="x-p"/> The first of the שׂרים, princes, i.e., chief ministers of state or dignitaries, mentioned here is not the commander-in-chief, as under the warlike reign of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16">2Sa 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23">2Sa 20:23</reference>), but, in accordance with the peaceful rule of Solomon, the administrator of the kingdom (or prime minister): “<hi type="italic">Azariah</hi> the son of Zadok was הכּהן,” i.e., not the priest, but the administrator of the kingdom, the representative of the king before the people; like כּהן in v. 5, where this word is interpreted by המּלך רעה, with this difference, however, arising from the article before כּהן, that <hi type="italic">Azariah</hi> was the <hi type="italic">Kohen par excellence</hi>, that is to say, held the first place among the confidential counsellors of the king, so that his dignity was such as befitted the office of an administrator of the kingdom. Compare the explanation of כּהן at 2Sa 8:18. The view of the Vulgate, Luther, and others, which has been revived by Thenius, namely, that כּהן is to be connected as a genitive with בּן־צדוק in opposition to the accents, “Azariah the son of Zadok the priest,” is incorrect, and does not even yield any sense, since the connection of these words with the following <hi type="italic">Elichoreph</hi>, etc., is precluded by the absence of the copula <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>, which would be indispensable if Azariah had held the same office as the two brothers Elichoreph and Achijah.<note placement="foot">The objection by which Thenius tries to set aside this argument, which has been already advanced by <hi type="italic">Houbigant</hi>, viz., that “if the first (Azariah) was not also a state scribe, the copula would be inserted, as it is everywhere else from v. 4 onwards when a new office is mentioned,” proves nothing at all, because the copula is also omitted in v. 3, where the new office of מזכּיר is introduced.</note> <div eID="gen4774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4775" type="x-p"/> Moreover, Azariah the son of Zadok cannot be a grandson of Zadok the high priest, i.e., a son of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok, as many infer from 1 Chr. 5:34-35 (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.8-1Chr.6.9">1Ch 6:8-9</reference>); for, apart from the fact that Zadok’s grandson can hardly have been old enough at the time for Solomon to invest him with the chief dignity in the kingdom, which would surely be conferred upon none but men of mature years, we can see no reason why the Azariah mentioned here should not be called the son of Ahimaaz. If the Zadok referred to here was the high priest of that name, Azariah can only have been a brother of Ahimaaz. And there is no real difficulty in the way, since the name Azariah occurs three times in the line of high priests (1 Chr. 5:36, 39), and therefore was by no means rare.
entries.e7080ce27f16f352b3253b5084315dd33b669c38: 1Ki 4:3 <hi type="italic">Elichoreph</hi> and <hi type="italic">Achijah</hi>, sons of <hi type="italic">Shisha</hi>, who had held the same office under David, were secretaries of state (ספרים: see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2Sa 8:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2Sa 20:25</reference>, where the different names שׁשׁא = שׁיא and שׂריה are also discussed). - <hi type="italic">Jehoshaphat</hi> the son of Ahilud was the chancellor, as he had already been in the time of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2Sa 8:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.24">2Sa 20:24</reference>). The rendering of Thenius, “whilst Jehoshaphat was chancellor,” is grammatically impossible.
entries.db5b7f03e201287eac10acb644342e2cff3fa53c: 1Ki 4:4 <div eID="gen4775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4776" type="x-p"/> On <hi type="italic">Benaiah</hi>, compare 1Ki 2:35 and the Commentary on 2Sa 23:20. On <hi type="italic">Zadok</hi> and <hi type="italic">Abiathar</hi>, see at 2Sa 8:17. It appears strange that Abiathar should be named as priest, i.e., as high priest, along with Zadok, since Solomon had deposed him from the priestly office (1Ki 2:27, 1Ki 2:35), and we cannot imagine any subsequent pardon. The only possible explanation is that proposed by Theodoret, namely, that Solomon had only deprived him of the ἀρχή, i.e., of the priest’s office, but not of the ἱερωσύνη or priestly dignity, because this was hereditary.<note placement="foot">Τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀφείλατο, ου ̓ τῆς ἱερωσύνης ἐγύμνωσεν· τὴν γὰρ τῆς ἱερωσύνης αξίαν οὐκ ἐκ χειροτονίας ἀλλ ̓ ἐκ γονικῆς εἶχον διαδοχῆς. - Theodoret.</note>
entries.eddea6be23709b0bd4133efcc3feb46394a7fb1f: 1Ki 4:5 <hi type="italic">Azariah</hi> the son of Nathan was over the נצּבים, i.e., the twelve officers named in vv. 7ff. <hi type="italic">Zabud</hi> the son of Nathan was כּהן (not the son of “Nathan the priest,” as Luther and many others render it). כּהן is explained by the epithet appended, המּלך רעה: privy councillor, i.e., confidential adviser of the king. Nathan is not the prophet of that name, as Thenius supposes, but the son of David mentioned in 2Sa 5:14. Azariah and Zabud were therefore nephews of Solomon.
entries.fa1070d75702ee859426c2a8fa2ecbe8ce828c73: 1Ki 4:6 <hi type="italic">Ahishar</hi> was הבּית על, over the palace, i.e., governor of the palace, or minister of the king’s household (compare 1Ki 16:9; 2Ki 18:18, and <reference osisRef="Isa.22.15">Isa 22:15</reference>), an office met with for the first time under Solomon. <hi type="italic">Adoniram</hi>, probably the same person as <hi type="italic">Adoram</hi> in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.24">2Sa 20:24</reference>, was chief overseer of the tributary service. He was so in the time of David also.
entries.62ee3a8a1c27ed1f8a31702f5d467d7c6b164f09: 1Ki 4:7 <div eID="gen4776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4777" type="x-p"/> Solomon’s Official Persons and Their Districts. - 1Ki 4:7. Solomon had (appointed) twelve נצּבים over all Israel, who provided (כּלכּלוּ) for the king and his house, i.e., supplied provisions for the necessities of the court. These prefects are not to be regarded as “chamberlains,” or administrators of the royal domains (Michaelis and Ewald), for these are mentioned in 1Ch 27:25. under a different title. They are “general receivers of taxes,” or “chief tax-collectors,” as Rosenmüller expresses it, who levied the king’s duties or taxes, which consisted in the East, as they still do to the present time, for the most part of natural productions, or the produce of the land, and not of money payments as in the West, and delivered them at the royal kitchen (Rosenmüller, A. <hi type="italic">und N. Morgenland</hi>, iii. p. 166). It cannot be inferred from the explanation given by Josephus, ἡγεμόνες καὶ στρατηγοί, that they exercised a kind of government, as Thenius supposes, since this explanation is nothing but a subjective conjecture. “One month in the year was it every one’s duty (אחד על יהיה) to provide.” The districts assigned to the twelve prefects coincide only partially with the territories of the tribes, because the land was probably divided among them according to its greater or smaller productiveness. Moreover, the order in which the districts are enumerated is not a geographical one, but probably follows the order in which the different prefects had to send the natural productions month by month for the maintenance of the king’s court. The description begins with Ephraim in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.8">1Ch 27:8</reference>, then passes over in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.9">1Ch 27:9</reference> to the territory of Dan to the west of it, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.10">1Ch 27:10</reference> to the territory of Judah and Simeon on the south, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.11">1Ch 27:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.12">1Ch 27:12</reference> to the territory of Manasseh on this side from the Mediterranean to the Jordan, then in vv. 13 and 14 to the territory of Manasseh on the other side of the Jordan, thence back again in vv. 15 and 16 to the northern parts of the land on this side, viz., the territories of Naphtali and Asher, and thence farther south to Issachar in v. 17, and Benjamin in v. 18, closing at last in v. 19 with Gilead.
entries.9872779544634a2ebabe577868c4256d2ef9aff1: 1Ki 4:8 <div eID="gen4777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4778" type="x-p"/> In the names of the prefects we are struck with the fact, that in the case of five of them the names given are not their own but their fathers’ names. It is very improbable that the proper names should have dropped out five times (as Clericus, Michaelis, and others suppose); and consequently there is simply the assumption left, that the persons in question bore their fathers’ names with <hi type="italic">Ben</hi> prefixed as their own proper names: <hi type="italic">Benhur, Bendeker</hi>, etc., after the analogy of <hi type="italic">Benchanan</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.20">1Ch 4:20</reference> and others, although such a proper name as <hi type="italic">Ben-Abinadab</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.11">1Ch 4:11</reference>) appears very strange. <hi type="italic">Benhur</hi> was stationed on the mountains of Ephraim. These mountains, here only the mountainous district of the tribe of Ephraim, were among the most fruitful portions of Palestine (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.14-Josh.17.15">Jos 17:14-15</reference>).
entries.ed20c1a52e841fc0e1586358871a0713462d1b93: 1Ki 4:9 <hi type="italic">Bendeker</hi> was in <hi type="italic">Makaz</hi>, a city only mentioned here, the situation of which is unknown, but which is at any rate to be sought for in the tribe of Dan, to which the other cities of this district belong. <hi type="italic">Shaalbim</hi> has probably been preserved in the present <hi type="italic">Selbit</hi>, to the north-west of <hi type="italic">Yâlo</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.42">Jos 19:42</reference>). <hi type="italic">Bethshemesh</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Ain-Shems</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.10">Jos 15:10</reference>). <hi type="italic">Elon</hi> (אילון), which is distinguished from <hi type="italic">Ajalon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.42">Jos 19:42</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference>) by the epithet <hi type="italic">Bethchanan</hi>, and belonged to the tribe of Dan, has not yet been discovered (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.43">Jos 19:43</reference>). The lxx have arbitrarily interpolated ἕως before <hi type="italic">Bethchanan</hi>, and Thenius naturally takes this under his protection, and consequently traces <hi type="italic">Bethchanan</hi> in the village of <hi type="italic">Beit Hunûn</hi> (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 371), but without considering that ἕως yields no reasonable sense unless preceded by מן, ἐκ (from; cf. 1Ki 4:12).
entries.90b228a606f90323741cda8792e01b04d0b9d2db: 1Ki 4:10 <hi type="italic">Benhesed</hi> was in <hi type="italic">Arubboth</hi>, which does not occur again, so that its situation, even if it should be identical with <hi type="italic">Arab</hi> in <reference osisRef="Josh.15.52">Jos 15:52</reference>, as Böttcher conjectures, can only be approximatively inferred from the localities which follow. To him (לו), i.e., to his district, belonged <hi type="italic">Sochoh</hi> and all the land of <hi type="italic">Hepher</hi>. From <hi type="italic">Sochoh</hi> we may see that Benhesed’s district was in the tribe of Judah. Of the two <hi type="italic">Sochohs</hi> in Judah, that still exist under the name of <hi type="italic">Shuweikeh</hi>, it is impossible to determine with certainty which is intended here, whether the one upon the mountains (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.48">Jos 15:48</reference>) or the one in the plain (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>). The fact that it is associated with the land of <hi type="italic">Hepher</hi> rather favours the latter. The land of <hi type="italic">Hepher</hi>, which must not be confounded with the city of <hi type="italic">Gath-hepher</hi> in the tribe of Zebulun (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.13">Jos 19:13</reference>; 2Ki 14:25), but was the territory of one of the Canaanitish kings who were defeated by Joshua, was probably situated in the plain (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.12.17">Jos 12:17</reference>).
entries.4284c8df8564c96ead3fe27aafa55a20b0937b99: 1Ki 4:11 <hi type="italic">Ben-Abinadab</hi> had the whole of the high range of Dor (דּאר נפת, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.23">Jos 12:23</reference>), i.e., the strip of coast on the Mediterranean Sea below the promontory of Carmel, where the city of <hi type="italic">Dor</hi>, which has been preserved in the village of <hi type="italic">Tantura</hi> or <hi type="italic">Tortura</hi>, nine miles to the north of Caesarea, was situated (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.2">Jos 11:2</reference>). Whether this district embraced the fruitful plain of Sharon is not so clearly made out as Thenius supposes. בּן־אבינדב stands at the head absolutely, without any grammatical connection with כּל־נפת: “Abinadab: the whole of the high range of Dor,” etc. The person named was probably a son of David’s eldest brother but one (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.8">1Sa 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.13">1Sa 17:13</reference>), and therefore Solomon’s cousin; and he had married Solomon’s daughter.
entries.93a2b5f640e3253fd4f8063dfeb22f55fd0abe4e: 1Ki 4:12 <hi type="italic">Baana</hi> the son of Ahilud was most likely a brother of Jehoshaphat the chancellor (1Ki 4:3). This district embraced the cities on the southern edge of the plain of Jezreel, and extended to the Jordan. Taanach and Megiddo, which have been preserved in the villages of <hi type="italic">Taanuk</hi> and <hi type="italic">Lejun</hi>, were situated on the south-western border of this plain, and belonged to the Manassites (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.12.21">Jos 12:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>). “And all Bethshean,” in other words, the whole of the district of Bethshean, i.e., Beisan, at the eastern end of the valley of Jezreel, where it opens into the Jordan valley (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal.</hi> ii. p. 740ff.), “which (district was situated) by the side of <hi type="italic">Zarthan</hi> below Jezreel, from (the town of) Bethshean (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.11">Jos 17:11</reference>) to Abel-Mecholah, on the other side of Jokmeam.” <hi type="italic">Zarthan</hi>, also called <hi type="italic">Zereda</hi> (compare 1Ki 7:46 with <reference osisRef="2Chr.4.17">2Ch 4:17</reference>), has probably been preserved, so far as the name is concerned, in <hi type="italic">Kurn Sartabeh</hi>, in the neighbourhood of which the old city probably stood, about five miles to the south of Beisan, at a point where the Jordan valley contracts (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.3.16">Jos 3:16</reference>). The expression “below Jezreel” refers to “all Bethshean,” and may be explained from the elevated situation of Jezreel, the present <hi type="italic">Zerîn</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.19.18">Jos 19:18</reference>). According to Rob. iii. p. 163, this is “comparatively high, and commands a wide and noble view, extending down the broad low valley on the east of Beisan and to the mountains of Ajlun beyond the Jordan.” The following words, “from Bethshean to Abel-Mecholah,” give a more precise definition of the boundary. The lxx have erroneously inserted καὶ before מבּית־שׁאן, and Thenius and Böttcher defend it on the strength of their erroneous interpretations of the preceding statements. <hi type="italic">Abel-Mecholah</hi> was in the Jordan valley, according to the <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>., ten Roman miles to the south of Beisan (see at Jdg 7:22). The last clause is not quite intelligible to us, as the situation of the Levitical city <hi type="italic">Jokmeam</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.53">1Ch 6:53</reference>, or <hi type="italic">Kibzaim</hi>, a different place from the <hi type="italic">Jokneam</hi> on Carmel, <reference osisRef="Josh.12.22">Jos 12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.34">Jos 21:34</reference>) has not yet been discovered (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.21.22">Jos 21:22</reference>). According to this, Baanah’s district in the Jordan valley did not extend so far as <hi type="italic">Kurn Sartabeh</hi>, but simply to the neighbourhood of Zarthan, and embraced the whole of the tribe-territory of Manasseh on this side of the Jordan.
entries.ed1c5bed8ef4e7adc7597a25865b912cecb86472: 1Ki 4:13 <div eID="gen4778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4779" type="x-p"/> Bengeber was in <hi type="italic">Ramoth</hi> of Gilead in the tribe of Gad (<reference osisRef="Josh.20.8">Jos 20:8</reference>), probably on the site of the modern <hi type="italic">Szalt</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.4.43">Deu 4:43</reference>). “To him belonged the <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi> (Jair’s-lives) in Gilead, to him the region of <hi type="italic">Argob</hi> in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and brazen bolts.” If we look at this passage alone, the region of Argob in Bashan appears to be distinct from the Havvoth Jair in Gilead. But if we compare it with Num 32:40-41; <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4-Deut.3.5">Deu 3:4-5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Josh.13.30">Jos 13:30</reference>, it is evident from these passages that the Jair’s-lives are identical with the sixty large and fortified cities of the region of Argob. For, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>, these sixty fortified cities, with high walls, gates, and bars, were all fortified cities of the kingdom of Og of Bashan, which the Israelites conquered under Moses, and to which, according to Num 32:41, Jair the Manassite, who had conquered them, gave the name of <hi type="italic">Havvoth Jair</hi>. Hence it is stated in <reference osisRef="Josh.13.30">Jos 13:30</reference>, that the sixty Jair-towns were situated in Bashan. Consequently the אר חבל לו in our verse is to be taken as a more precise definition of וגו יאיר חוּת לו, or a clearer description of the district superintended by <hi type="italic">Bengeber</hi>, so that <hi type="italic">Gilead</hi> is used, as is frequently the case, in the broader sense of <hi type="italic">Peraea</hi>. Compare with this the Commentary on <reference osisRef="Deut.3.4">Deu 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.13">Deu 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.3.14">Deu 3:14</reference>, where the names ארגּב and חוּת are explained, and the imaginary discrepancy between the sixty Jair’s-towns in the passages cited, and the twenty-three and thirty cities of Jair in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.22">1Ch 2:22</reference> and Jdg 10:4, is discussed and solved. And when Thenius objects to this explanation on the ground that the villages of Jair cannot be identical with the sixty fortified cities, because villages of nomads and strongly fortified cities could not be one and the same, this objection falls to the ground with the untenable interpretation of חוּת as applying to nomad villages.
entries.79acae66c9acc943f802a8364d7f3149afe1c9ff: 1Ki 4:14 <hi type="italic">Ahinadab</hi> the son of Iddo received as his district <hi type="italic">Mahanaim</hi>, a fortified and probably also a very important city to the north of the Jabbok, on the border of the tribe of Gad, which may perhaps have been preserved in the ruin of <hi type="italic">Mahneh</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.13.26">Jos 13:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.32.3">Gen 32:3</reference>). מחנימה, to Mahanaim (cf. Ewald, §216, <hi type="italic">a</hi>., note), with ה local, probably referring to the fact that Ahinadab was sent away to Mahanaim.
entries.d50230c168cdf48d1c0be36a71ba60e44cc771e6: 1Ki 4:15 <hi type="italic">Ahimaaz</hi>, possibly Zadok’s son (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.27">2Sa 15:27</reference>; 2Sa 17:17.), in <hi type="italic">Naphtali</hi>.
